title: Sam Altman renews his ‘democratic AI’ pitch as Anthropic holds a harder line

content_html:
Sam Altman has a preferred way of framing the contest over artificial intelligence, and it is a stark one. Either the United States and its allies build the technology and spread its benefits, the OpenAI chief has argued, or authoritarian governments use it to cement and expand their own power.

That binary, set out most fully in a 2024 Washington Post op-ed and carried into his appearances before Congress since, is the spine of what he calls “democratic AI”.

A recent Business Insider piece places the argument beside a quieter friction with Anthropic, whose chief executive Dario Amodei has been pushing a US-led AI coalition on notably different terms. The two men agree on the threat. What separates them is the remedy, and increasingly the register in which they make it.

Altman’s prescription leans on scale and openness. He wants more data centres and the power to run them, clearer rules on foreign investment, and a democratic system that reaches allied nations before an authoritarian one does.

On openness, OpenAI has something to point to. Its gpt-oss models, released in August 2025, were the company’s first open-weight systems in years, a pair of models that anyone can download and run rather than access through a paid interface.

For the democratic-AI case, that matters, because open weights are the version of the technology that actually travels to allied developers and governments. The gesture still sat awkwardly against OpenAI’s absence from an industry letter backing American open models.

Altman has paired that with a call for shared rules. He has floated an international body to set AI norms, comparing it loosely to the organisation that governs internet domain names, and has told lawmakers the state should fund safety testing rather than gate models behind approvals.

Amodei has taken the harder line on the hardware underneath all of it. In a January 2025 essay written after China’s DeepSeek unsettled markets with a cheaply trained model, he argued that “well-enforced export controls are the only thing that can prevent China from getting millions of chips”.

A more efficient model, he wrote, was no reason to loosen the rules. If anything, he read DeepSeek as evidence that the controls were doing their job.Sam Altman casts the AI race as democracies versus authoritarians. Dario Amodei’s Anthropic wants tighter chip export controls, not looser ones.

The backdrop is a US regime of chip export controls that has tightened repeatedly, with officials moving to close the loopholes that let advanced processors reach Chinese firms through overseas subsidiaries. Amodei sits at the hawkish end of that debate, framing strict controls as the difference between a unipolar and a bipolar world, language that treats the flow of chips as close to the whole game.

Altman’s framing is broader and, his critics would say, more convenient for OpenAI. His “commercial diplomacy” pitch pairs export controls with the active export of American AI to friendly states, which is also a fair description of OpenAI’s addressable market. He has said the values a technology carries travel with it, and that spreading a democratic version abroad is itself a security measure.

Anthropic’s bet runs the other way. Keep the most powerful hardware scarce, keep the frontier concentrated among a handful of accountable labs, and treat wide distribution as a risk to be managed rather than a race to be won. It is a safety argument and a competitive one at the same time, and Amodei has rarely pretended otherwise.

Neither posture is free of self-interest, and Business Insider is careful to note that the sharper contrast is partly the observer’s. Altman benefits from a world hungry for American models, and Anthropic benefits from one where being cautious and hard to copy counts as a moat.

What is clear is that the two most closely watched labs in the country now describe the same race in different vocabularies. One talks about spreading AI in order to win it. The other talks about withholding the chips that make it possible.

content_html_zh:
萨姆·奥尔特曼（Sam Altman）有一种偏爱的方式来构建人工智能竞赛，而且是一种鲜明的方式。 这位 OpenAI 负责人认为，要么是美国及其盟友开发这项技术并传播其好处，要么独裁政府利用它来巩固和扩大自己的权力。

这种二元论在 2024 年《华盛顿邮报》的一篇专栏文章中得到了最全面的阐述，并自此在国会露面时得以体现，它是他所谓的“民主人工智能”的支柱。

《商业内幕》最近的一篇文章将这一论点与 Anthropic 之间较小的摩擦放在一起，Anthropic 的首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 一直在以明显不同的条款推动美国领导的人工智能联盟。 两人对威胁的看法一致。 他们的区别在于补救措施，而且越来越多的是他们进行补救措施的寄存器。

奥特曼的处方依赖于规模和开放性。 他希望有更多的数据中心和运行这些数据中心的权力，更明确的外国投资规则，以及一个比独裁国家更早到达盟国的民主制度。

在开放性方面，OpenAI 有其可取之处。 其 gpt-oss 模型于 2025 年 8 月发布，是该公司多年来的第一个开放权重系统，任何人都可以下载和运行这两个模型，而不是通过付费界面访问。

对于民主人工智能的情况来说，这很重要，因为开放权重是实际传播到联盟开发商和政府的技术版本。 与 OpenAI 缺席支持美国开放模式的行业信函相比，这一姿态仍然显得尴尬。

奥特曼同时呼吁制定共同规则。 他提出了一个国际机构来制定人工智能规范，将其与管理互联网域名的组织进行了松散的比较，并告诉立法者，国家应该资助安全测试，而不是为批准背后的模型提供资金。

Amodei 在所有底层硬件上采取了更强硬的路线。 在中国的 DeepSeek 以廉价训练的模型扰乱市场后，他在 2025 年 1 月发表的一篇文章中指出，“严格执行的出口管制是唯一可以阻止中国获得数百万芯片的方法”。

他写道，更有效的模型并不是放松规则的理由。 如果说有什么不同的话，他认为 DeepSeek 是控制装置发挥作用的证据。萨姆·奥尔特曼 (Sam Altman) 将人工智能竞赛视为民主国家与独裁国家的较量。 达里奥·阿莫代 (Dario Amodei) 的 Anthropic 希望加强而不是放松芯片出口管制。

背景是美国的芯片出口管制制度一再收紧，官员们正在努力堵住先进处理器通过海外子公司到达中国公司的漏洞。 阿莫代在这场辩论中处于鹰派立场，他将严格控制视为单极世界和两极世界之间的区别，将筹码流视为与整个游戏密切相关的语言。

Altman 的框架更广泛，他的批评者会说，这对 OpenAI 来说更方便。 他的“商业外交”主张将出口管制与美国人工智能向友好国家的积极出口结合起来，这也是对 OpenAI 潜在市场的公平描述。 他曾表示，一项技术所承载的价值会随之传播，而在国外传播民主版本本身就是一种安全措施。

Anthropic 的赌注却相反。 保持最强大的硬件稀缺，将前沿集中在少数负责任的实验室中，并将广泛分布视为需要管理的风险，而不是一场需要获胜的竞赛。 这是一种安全论点，同时也是一种竞争性论点，阿莫代很少假装不是这样。

这两种态度都不是出于自身利益，《商业内幕》谨慎地指出，这种鲜明的对比部分是观察者的。 奥特曼受益于渴望美国模式的世界，而人类则受益于谨慎且难以复制的护城河。

显而易见的是，该国两个最受关注的实验室现在用不同的词汇描述同一种族。 有人谈到传播人工智能以赢得胜利。 另一个则谈到扣留使其成为可能的芯片。
